items.title: 30Y up, 2Y down on the same Fed day -- never happened before
items.idea: On today's FOMC decision, 30-year Treasury yields rose while 2-year yields fell -- the first time this exact divergence has occurred on a Fed decision day since data begins in August 1987, per @ljkawa. That's extreme bear-steepening: the front end is pricing no near-term hike risk while the long end reprices term premium and inflation risk.
items.angle: Three separate sources in this window converge on the same tail: the 30Y hit its highest close since 2007 today (see Robert's Inn and Neil Sethi items). When that many independent observers land on the same number, it's signal, not noise.
items.tweetA: 30Y yields rose while 2Y fell on the same Fed decision. Hasn't happened once since 1987. The bond market just told Warsh his 'hold' wasn't dovish -- it was a permission slip for an inflation risk premium.
items.tweetB: Three different newsletters flagged the 30Y hitting its highest close since 2007 today, independently. When that many unrelated observers converge on the same tail of the curve, that's not noise, that's the market pricing a policy mistake.

charts.desc: US30Y vs US2Y yield chart around today's FOMC decision -- first-ever divergence of this magnitude since Aug 1987 data begins.

items.title: This BTC bear market is shallow but it hasn't run its course in time
items.idea: Glassnode's Week Onchain: the current cycle's Bitcoin drawdown is shallower in magnitude than even the mildest prior bear market, but it hasn't lasted nearly as long in duration as its predecessors -- an argument for patience over calling a bottom based on depth alone.
items.angle: Depth says 'buy the dip,' duration says 'not yet.' Worth watching against any 'bottom is in' calls circulating this week -- the time-based argument is the one bulls keep skipping.
items.tweetA: This BTC drawdown is milder than every prior bear market -- but it also hasn't lasted nearly as long. Depth says buy, duration says not yet. Glassnode's chart is the one to save before you average in.
items.tweetB: Everyone comparing this cycle's BTC drawdown % to prior bottoms and declaring the bottom in is using the wrong axis. It's time, not depth, that's the tell -- and by that measure this one isn't close to done.

charts.desc: Glassnode chart comparing this cycle's BTC drawdown depth and duration against every prior bear market.

items.title: Retail just posted its biggest one-day stock-selling since COVID
items.idea: Retail investors sold a net $243 million of single stocks yesterday -- the largest one-day retail outflow since the COVID crash, per Vanda data via @KevRGordon.
items.angle: This lands the same day Goldman's prime brokerage desk clocked the largest hedge-fund de-gross since Nov 2022 (see the Dark Side of the Boom item below). Retail and hedge funds capitulated in the same window -- an unusual double-signal.
items.tweetA: Retail dumped $243M of single stocks yesterday -- the biggest one-day outflow since COVID. Pair that with Goldman's prime broker data showing the largest hedge-fund de-gross since Nov 2022, and both cohorts of buyers went to cash at the same moment.
items.tweetB: Retail capitulating the same day hedge funds ran their biggest de-gross in four years is either the flush before the bounce, or confirmation nobody wants to own this tape heading into August's seasonally worst outflow window.

charts.desc: Vanda retail single-stock flow chart showing the largest one-day net-sell since the COVID crash.

items.title: Semis: 4th cheapest sector, highest expected growth -- 22% cheaper than Staples
items.idea: If semis were classified as their own sector, they'd be the 4th cheapest in the market while also carrying the highest expected 12-month earnings growth rate of any sector -- 22.1% cheaper than Consumer Staples, per Chart Kid Matt.
items.angle: This is the valuation counter-argument to the 'AI trade is broken' narrative dominating three other items in this window. Cheap plus fastest-growing is historically an unstable combination.
items.tweetA: Semis are the 4th cheapest sector in the market with the highest expected earnings growth of any sector -- 22% cheaper than Staples. Every other headline today says the AI trade is broken. The valuation data says something else.
items.tweetB: Cheap plus fastest-growing is not a stable equilibrium. Either the growth estimates are wrong or the multiple re-rates higher. Semis screening this way after a 5%+ one-day drop in SOX is the setup, not the confirmation.

charts.desc: Sector valuation-vs-growth scatter showing Semis as the 4th cheapest sector with the highest expected earnings growth.

items.title: Under the index-level selloff, breadth is quietly repairing
items.idea: 'More stocks are moving into healthy uptrends,' per Grant Hawkridge -- a breadth-repair signal building beneath a falling headline index on the same day the Nasdaq-100 entered correction territory.
items.angle: Worth tracking against the semis valuation item above: two separate breadth/valuation signals both point away from the 'market is broadly weak' framing that most of today's other newsletters lead with.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq-100 just closed in correction territory. Under the surface, more individual stocks are rotating into healthy uptrends. That divergence is either rotation working exactly as it should, or a head-fake before breadth breaks too.
items.tweetB: Everyone's trading the index headline today. The stock-level data says the average name is healthier than the tape it's sitting inside. Breadth repairing under a falling index is usually a late-stage signal, not an early one.

charts.desc: Percentage of S&P names in confirmed uptrends, rebuilding even as the headline index falls.

items.title: Gold broke the triangle bears called for $3,000s -- it broke up instead
items.idea: Gold broke out of a multi-month triangle pattern that bearish commentators expected to resolve toward the $3,000s; instead it broke upward and now holds the $3,900-4,100 support zone (formed at the Oct-Nov 2025 lows), with $4,300-4,600 as the next resistance test. Silver's own triangle breakout remains intact, needing a clear move above $60-70 to confirm. Spot gold rose ~1% and silver ~1% on today's Fed hold even as equities sold off sharply.
items.angle: Pairs directly with Robert's Inn's gold-miner buy call below -- two independent sources turning bullish precious metals into a low-volume summer window ahead of September catalysts (PCE, Fed).

charts.desc: Charts inside -- worth opening (gold/silver triangle breakout and support/resistance zone charts).

items.tweetA: Gold broke a triangle everyone expected to resolve toward $3,000. It resolved UP instead. $3,900-4,100 is now support; $4,300-4,600 is the next test. The bears who called the top in July are the same ones who'll chase it in September.
items.tweetB: Precious metals barely moved on a hawkish Fed hold and a fresh Iran escalation in the same week. That's not weakness -- that's a market that's already priced in max pessimism with nowhere left to fall.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: 3 of 12 FOMC voters wanted to hike today -- on a meeting priced as a lock to hold
items.idea: The Fed held at 3.50-3.75% but with three dissents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) favoring a 25bp hike -- an unusually contentious vote for a meeting the market treated as settled. Goldman read Warsh's comments as dovish (higher market rates already doing some of the Fed's tightening), but the curve gave a split verdict: front end down, long end up on rising breakevens. Markets now price ~60% odds of a September hike, though Goldman itself expects the Fed stays on hold through year-end on softer core inflation.
items.angle: The 3-dissent vote is the real story, not the hold itself -- a committee this divided rarely stays quiet for long, and September is now genuinely live.
items.tweetA: 3 of 12 FOMC voters wanted a hike TODAY on a meeting priced as a lock to hold. That's not consensus, that's a fault line. September's 60% hike odds are the market pricing that fault line to crack.
items.tweetB: Warsh's own committee just told you the Fed put isn't automatic -- three hawks dissented in favor of tightening into an AI capex boom and an oil shock. If you're still trading this like 2021 easy money, re-read the vote count.

charts.desc: No charts in email; likely a dissent/vote breakdown in the full post.

items.title: OpenAI nears 1B weekly users -- but only 5% pay, and Anthropic out-earns it anyway
items.idea: OpenAI is closing in on 1 billion weekly active users (vs. Google's claimed 950 million monthly, announced days earlier) -- but only about 50 million (5%) are paying ChatGPT subscribers. OpenAI now says roughly 50% of its business is enterprise, chasing Anthropic's enterprise lead built on Claude Code and Claude Cowork, where Anthropic already runs a higher annualized revenue run-rate than OpenAI off a smaller total user base.
items.angle: The vanity metric is the billion-user headline; the real story is that scale and monetization are decoupling -- Anthropic is out-earning OpenAI's enterprise push with fewer total users.
items.tweetA: OpenAI: near 1B weekly users, only 50M pay (5% conversion). Anthropic: smaller user base, higher revenue run-rate. Scale and monetization are decoupling in real time, and the market is still valuing both companies on the scale number.
items.tweetB: Google says 950M monthly users. OpenAI says nearly 1B weekly. Different metrics, same PR instinct: whoever picks the denominator wins the headline. Ignore both -- watch enterprise revenue per user, that's where Anthropic is actually winning.

items.title: SK hynix: profit +550%, margins at 83% -- stock down 10%, a million Korean accounts margin-called
items.idea: SK hynix posted revenue +257% YoY, operating profit +550% YoY, and 83% gross margins (software-like) -- yet the stock fell roughly 9-10% on a 'beat but not enough' reaction, triggering margin calls for over a million Korean retail traders running leveraged ETF bets on hynix and Samsung. Parekh frames this against 'RAMageddon' -- memory supply so tight the industry is effectively sold out through the end of the decade.
items.angle: A totally different angle on SK hynix than the earnings-prep newsletters covering it today -- this one is about retail leverage carnage in Korea, not the supply/demand fundamentals.
items.tweetA: SK hynix: revenue +257%, operating profit +550%, gross margin 83% -- and the stock dropped 10% and wiped out a million leveraged Korean retail accounts. When 'beat but not enough' triggers a margin-call cascade, the position sizing was the actual risk, not the earnings.
items.tweetB: Memory is sold out through the end of the decade (RAMageddon), hynix margins are software-like, and the stock still sold off on the print. That gap between fundamentals and price reaction is exactly where the next leg gets built -- assuming you weren't levered into it.

items.title: Stripe reportedly offering 70x revenue for OpenRouter
items.idea: Stripe is reportedly negotiating to buy OpenRouter (~$140M revenue) for roughly $10B -- about 70x revenue, well above the 22-23x revenue Elon paid for Cursor via SpaceX/xAI right before the SpaceX IPO.
items.angle: Private AI M&A multiples are expanding the same week hedge funds ran their biggest public-tech de-gross since 2016 -- private and public AI valuations are pulling in opposite directions, and that spread doesn't hold indefinitely.
items.tweetA: Stripe reportedly offering 70x revenue for OpenRouter. Elon paid 22x for Cursor. Same week hedge funds ran their biggest tech de-gross since 2022 in public AI names. Private AI multiples are moving the opposite direction of public ones -- that spread doesn't hold forever.
items.tweetB: $10B for a company doing $140M in revenue is a bet on strategic option value, not the P&L. Fine if you're Stripe with a $150B balance sheet. Not fine if you're extrapolating that multiple onto anything trading on a public tape this week.

items.title: DoorDash gets FAA clearance for its own delivery drones
items.idea: DoorDash received an FAA nod for commercial delivery drones, joining (and outpacing) Amazon's now-tempered drone delivery push. Parekh notes the real use case is rural, not urban -- 15-30 minute one-way delivery windows where drones save meaningful time, unlike dense cities where human couriers are already fast.
items.angle: A small but real regulatory unlock for a physical-world logistics story that gets none of the attention AI software gets -- worth flagging as a slow-build infrastructure theme.
items.tweetA: DoorDash just got an FAA nod for its own delivery drones. Nobody's pricing this because it's 'just drones,' but the FAA clearance is the actual unlock -- regulatory approval is always the slower-moving constraint than the hardware.
items.tweetB: The drone delivery pitch keeps failing in cities because human couriers are already fast there. The real market is rural 20-30 minute one-way routes -- a smaller, boring-sounding TAM that's actually where the unit economics work.

items.title: Warsh dodged the one question that mattered -- and stocks sold off in real time
items.idea: Asked directly which inflation measure he targets, Warsh gave what Fed Guy Joseph Wang called a 'word salad' non-answer, refusing to name anything beyond 'core PCE plus a broader set of data' -- markets rolled over and closed at session lows specifically during that exchange. The author argues the Fed is trapped between 125% debt-to-GDP, $2T deficits, and positive real yields, and expects the next crisis to rhyme with March 2020 (forced Fed intervention, effectively yield curve control). He's actively buying gold miners now, citing Agnico Eagle's record $1.34B quarterly free cash flow and 50% YoY net income growth despite miners trading as if gold is heading lower.
items.angle: The most aggressive 'yield curve control is coming' call in this window -- a distinct, higher-conviction macro regime thesis worth separating from the more measured Dark Side of the Boom pieces.
items.tweetA: A reporter asked Warsh which inflation measure he targets. He didn't answer -- gave what Fed Guy called a 'word salad.' Stocks sold off in real time during that non-answer. When the Fed chair can't name his own target, that's the tell, not the hold.
items.tweetB: 125% debt-to-GDP, $2T deficits, positive real yields. That combination doesn't resolve quietly -- it resolves the way March 2020 did, with the Fed forced back into the Treasury market. Gold miners trading at a 40% discount to their own free cash flow are pricing none of that.

charts.desc: Charts inside -- worth opening (SPY 5-minute and QQQ daily charts around the Warsh presser).

items.title: Crypto's CLARITY Act just lost the one resource it can't buy back: Senate floor time
items.idea: The Senate advanced the Graham Russia-Iran sanctions bill 86-12, pushing the crypto market-structure CLARITY Act further down the floor-time queue. The real Democratic sticking point is ethics language covering the Trump family's disclosed $1.4B in crypto revenue -- Sen. Alsobrooks says she'll oppose the bill without stronger enforcement than a DOJ-only model. Separately, banks are pushing to restrict stablecoin reward/yield features that could pull deposits out of the regulated banking system.
items.angle: A distinct crypto-regulatory-plumbing angle nobody else in this window covered -- floor time, not political will, is the actual scarce resource holding CLARITY back.
items.tweetA: CLARITY Act had 15-9 committee support and passed the House 294-134. It's still stuck -- because Senate floor time this week went to Russia-Iran sanctions instead. The crypto bill isn't dying on the merits, it's dying on the calendar.
items.tweetB: The real veto point on crypto market-structure legislation isn't crypto policy -- it's a disclosed $1.4B in Trump-family crypto revenue that Democrats can't wave through with a DOJ-only ethics clause. Watch the ethics language, not the stablecoin language, to know if this passes in September.

items.title: Meta missed, Microsoft beat -- same night, same 'Mag 7' bucket, opposite reactions
items.idea: S&P -1.5%, Nasdaq -1.7%, Dow -2.2%, Russell -1.6%, all near session lows; Nasdaq-100 closed in correction territory. SOX fell 5.3% in the session, on pace for its worst month since 2001. After the close, Meta sold off on a miss and weak revenue guide while Microsoft rallied on top-and-bottom-line beats with cloud growth above expectations. WTI rose 6%+ after Trump vowed to strike Iran again following an attack on a US base in Jordan.
items.angle: The Meta/Microsoft divergence on the same earnings night is the real stock-picker's story inside a 'risk-off' macro day -- big tech is bifurcating, not moving as a bloc.
items.tweetA: Meta missed and guided weak. Microsoft beat on both lines with cloud ahead of expectations. Same earnings night, same 'Mag 7' bucket, opposite stock reactions. The index-level narrative just stopped applying to the index's own biggest members.
items.tweetB: SOX down 5.3% in a session, on pace for its worst month since 2001 -- while WTI ripped 6%+ on renewed Iran strikes. Oil up, semis down, same day: that's a stagflation-shaped tape, not a normal risk-off day.

items.title: There aren't enough electricians to hand-build the AI buildout -- so Vertiv's take doubled to $7M/MW
items.idea: SemiAnalysis tracks 61GW of modular/prefab datacenter capacity across 1,000+ sites and projects 30%+ of live capacity will be modular by end-2028. The driver is a hard labor bottleneck -- electricians represent 30-40% of construction man-hours, with the shortage most acute in Texas and Ohio starting 2027. Modular construction compresses build time ~36% (7-9 months) and runs ~8% cheaper per MW, while letting full-stack vendors like Vertiv expand captured content per project from ~$3.5M/MW to ~$7M/MW.
items.angle: The labor shortage is functioning as a forced subsidy toward full-stack modular vendors (Vertiv, Schneider) right as credit markets start questioning how the same capex gets financed (see the AI Credit item below).
items.tweetA: Vertiv's content capture per MW just went from $3.5M to $7M -- not because they sell more stuff, but because there physically aren't enough electricians to hand-build the AI datacenter buildout. The labor shortage is a forced vertical-integration subsidy for full-stack vendors.
items.tweetB: Electricians are 30-40% of datacenter construction hours, and SemiAnalysis models a shortage hitting Texas and Ohio hardest by 2027 -- exactly where the AI buildout concentrates. Modularization isn't a cost optimization here, it's the only way the capex plans are physically achievable at all.

charts.desc: Charts inside -- worth opening (labor demand-vs-supply by state, modular cost/time comparison charts).

items.title: Torsten Slok is naming names: Oracle and CoreWeave CDS spreads are the widest in AI-linked credit
items.idea: Apollo's Torsten Slok flags widening CDS spreads across AI-linked names, with Oracle and CoreWeave standing out, as the AI buildout shifts from internally-funded to debt-funded. Falling token prices and rising Chinese-model market share raise the usage volume needed to justify capex even as unit economics compress. The piece frames four open questions: whether ROI arrives in time, how the buildout gets financed, whether compute demand is truly limitless, and what happens if the payoff is merely delayed rather than cancelled.
items.angle: The most precise 'who's actually exposed' framing in this window -- Oracle and CoreWeave named specifically as the debt-financed pressure points, distinct from the equity-side 'AI trade is broken' framing everywhere else today.
items.tweetA: Torsten Slok is naming names: Oracle and CoreWeave CDS spreads are the widest in the AI-linked credit complex. Equity investors are still debating 'is AI overhyped.' Credit investors already moved past that question to 'who's funding the gap and what's the collateral.'
items.tweetB: Falling token prices are bullish for AI adoption and bearish for whoever just spent a trillion dollars building the infrastructure to sell those tokens. Slok's framing: the industry may be finishing a toll road just as the toll gets competed to zero.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Iran and the Houthis are testing a toll system on two chokepoints at once -- and China is buying an exemption
items.idea: Beyond the Hormuz standoff, the Houthis (per Reuters, with alleged IRGC technical assistance) are reportedly weighing a toll on commercial vessels transiting Bab el-Mandeb -- mirroring Iran's own claim to a Hormuz passage fee. Only 11 vessels transited the strait on Sunday, the lowest in months. China is separately negotiating direct passage guarantees with the Houthis for its own shipping, raising the prospect of a selective toll regime where Chinese and Russian-linked vessels pass free while Western and Saudi-linked shipping pays or gets attacked.
items.angle: An underappreciated tail risk that raises freight and insurance costs without needing a single barrel of lost output, and structurally favors China's shipping relationships over the West's.
items.tweetA: The oil story isn't 'production shut in' anymore -- it's Iran and the Houthis testing whether they can charge a toll on two chokepoints at once, Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. China is quietly negotiating a carve-out so its own ships pass free. That's not a supply shock, that's a new geopolitical tax on non-Chinese trade.
items.tweetB: 11 vessels transited Bab el-Mandeb on Sunday, the lowest in months, without a single ship being sunk. You don't need to close a strait to break it. A believable threat to insurers is enough, and insurers already priced it before the oil market did.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Same-size oil shock as March/April, much smaller dollar move -- here's why
items.idea: The dollar's usual reaction to rising oil (energy-exporter FX up, importer FX down) has been much weaker in July's escalation versus the March/April shock, because broader risk assets haven't sold off in sympathy this time and because front-end rate differentials set earlier in the year never fully reversed even as oil first fell then rebounded.
items.angle: Pairs with the Hormuz/Bab el-Mandeb item above -- explains why the FX market isn't screaming about an oil shock that credit and equity markets are already reacting to.
items.tweetA: Same size oil shock as March/April, much smaller dollar move. The difference isn't the commodity, it's that equities and credit haven't panicked alongside it this time. Oil beta into FX is dead until risk assets crack -- watch credit spreads, not the oil chart, for the dollar signal.
items.tweetB: Rate differentials set by the FIRST energy shock this year never fully unwound, even after oil pulled back. FX is trading the memory of an inflation scare more than the live commodity print. That's a sticky policy-expectations effect, not a real-time correlation.

items.title: PE portfolio-company CEO turnover has sat at 60-70% for 15 years -- nobody's fixing the actual problem
items.idea: 62% of European PE-portfolio company CEOs are first-time CEOs, and overall PE portfolio-company CEO turnover has held at 60-70% for 15 years, with most replacements happening in the first few years of ownership. McKinsey's research across ~300 PE-backed CEOs identifies onboarding excellence, stakeholder management, and personal learning velocity as what separates outperformers, and argues sponsors should shift spend from external CEO search ('buy') toward structured internal development ('build').
items.angle: A quiet but real signal for anyone tracking the PE-backed IPO/exit pipeline -- 60-70% CEO turnover is a direct, underpriced drag on exit timing and multiple.
items.tweetA: 60-70% CEO turnover at PE-backed companies, unchanged for 15 years. Sponsors spend enormous effort picking the right CEO and almost none developing the one they already have. That's a fifteen-year-old inefficiency sitting in plain sight in every PE playbook.
items.tweetB: 62% of European PE-portfolio CEOs are first-timers in the role. If you're underwriting a PE-backed IPO or credit deal, CEO tenure risk is a bigger variable than most models price -- a 6-12 month search vacuum during a leverage-sensitive period isn't free.

items.title: Largest hedge-fund de-gross since Nov 2022, triggered by one 'good but not perfect' Korean print
items.idea: Meta's 2026 capex guide moved from $125-145B to a floor of $130B even as the stock sold off on a miss. The piece argues the AI trade is shifting from a demand story to a financing story: Goldman's prime-brokerage data shows the largest 3-day hedge-fund de-gross since November 2022 and the largest 3-session tech long-selling in the bank's data back to 2016 -- both triggered initially by SK hynix's earnings reaction rippling from Korea into the US and Europe.
items.angle: The connective-tissue piece tying together SK hynix, the AI credit CDS story, and the Fed's hawkish hold into one 'AI cost of capital' theme -- today's dominant meta-narrative across four-plus sources in this window.
items.tweetA: Largest 3-day hedge-fund de-gross since November 2022. Largest 3-session tech long-selling since 2016. Both triggered by one 'not perfect enough' Korean earnings report. Positioning was so extended that a beat-but-not-flawless quarter unwound two years of gross leverage in 72 hours.
items.tweetB: For three years the question was 'how big can AI demand get.' The new question, forming in real time across four different newsletters today: 'who's paying the financing cost while we wait to find out.' That's a genuinely different market regime, not a dip.

items.title: FanDuel admitted its federal prediction market is a placeholder -- states just got their best legal argument
items.idea: DraftKings, FanDuel, and Fanatics have each built federally-regulated prediction-market products (via CME, Crypto.com, or DraftKings' own acquired Railbird exchange) specifically to offer sports contracts in states where their own sportsbooks are banned. FanDuel has said explicitly it will withdraw the product once a state legalizes sports betting -- an admitted placeholder. The appellate circuit split sits at 1-0 federal (Third Circuit/NJ) against a 4-7 trial-court lean toward states; the Sixth Circuit hears Tennessee/Ohio arguments tomorrow. 2025 legal sports betting handle hit $166.94B, more than double the combined revenue of the US movie, music, book, and museum industries.
items.angle: The sportsbooks openly admitting the federal exchange is a placeholder is effectively a confession of regulatory arbitrage that could sink the Kalshi/Polymarket appellate momentum their whole model depends on.
items.tweetA: FanDuel said out loud that its federal prediction-market product is a placeholder it'll withdraw once state sports betting is legal. That's not a legal argument, that's a confession -- and it's now Exhibit A for every state AG arguing this is jurisdictional arbitrage dressed up as innovation.
items.tweetB: $166.94B in legal sports betting handle in 2025 -- more than movies, music, books, and museums combined. Kalshi and Polymarket picked this fight over principle. The sportsbooks joined because the market is too large to sit out, and that's exactly what makes a Supreme Court date inevitable.

items.title: AI resume screening can discriminate by age without anyone coding it to
items.idea: AI hiring/resume-screening tools trained mostly on younger, recently-hired employee data can learn to flag long job gaps or 20+-year-old graduation dates as red flags without anyone explicitly programming age discrimination. Under the ADEA, a 'facially neutral' algorithmic process that disproportionately screens out over-40 applicants can still be illegal even without discriminatory intent.
items.angle: A quiet but real legal-exposure story for every company that adopted an AI applicant-tracking vendor this year -- disparate-impact liability doesn't require intent, and most HR teams never audit their vendor's training data.
items.tweetA: An AI hiring tool doesn't need to be told to discriminate by age to do it -- training data skewed toward recently-hired, younger employees is enough. The ADEA doesn't care about intent, only disparate impact. Every company that outsourced resume screening to a vendor this year inherited legal exposure it probably hasn't audited.
items.tweetB: The AI hiring story everyone covers is 'AI screens resumes faster.' The one nobody covers: faster screening on biased training data just compounds a discrimination problem at algorithmic speed instead of catching it one bad recruiter at a time.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Goldman's flow desk: August ties May as the worst month for equity outflows
items.idea: Goldman's flow desk flags August as tied with May for the worst month of the year for equity outflows from mutual funds and ETFs. July's de-gross already cleaned up positioning, but gross leverage remains elevated enough for another shock to force further liquidation. Corporate buybacks are the main near-term demand cushion -- over 90% of S&P 500 names should be back in open buyback windows by mid-August. The desk favors reverse dispersion, IWM puts, and retail-favorite optionality as protection into rising single-stock correlation (Corr1) risk.
items.angle: Pairs directly with the retail-selling and hedge-fund de-grossing items above -- three sources converging on the same 'who's the marginal buyer in August' question.
items.tweetA: Goldman's own flow desk: August ties May as the worst seasonal month for equity outflows, and the main demand cushion left is buybacks reopening for 90%+ of the S&P by mid-August. If earnings season doesn't deliver a clean beat streak before those windows reopen, there's a real air pocket in between.
items.tweetB: Goldman is telling clients to buy correlation protection -- IWM puts, reverse dispersion -- into August specifically because gross leverage is still elevated after the July de-gross. Translation: the flush wasn't big enough to make the desk feel safe yet.

items.title: CVNA: 40% volume growth and near-investment-grade credit -- with zero open-market insider buying
items.idea: Carvana guided toward ~200K retail units (+39.6% YoY) and a record ~$670M GAAP operating income (+31% YoY) for Q2, with net debt/EBITDA improving toward ~1.0x, near investment-grade, even as retail GPU compresses YoY on narrower wholesale-retail spreads and the lapse of prior tariff benefits (~$100/unit headwind). Notably, the CFO, COO, and 10%-owner Ernest Garcia II have all executed large 10b5-1 sales and covered-call monetizations (Garcia alone collected $272M in option premiums at $450-500 strikes) with zero open-market purchases recorded.
items.angle: The fundamentals are genuinely strong, but the total absence of insider buying against large structured insider selling is the tell worth watching into the print.
items.tweetA: Carvana: +40% unit growth, EBITDA at a record, net debt/EBITDA heading toward investment-grade. Also Carvana: the CFO, COO, and 10%-owner insider have been steadily selling via 10b5-1 plans and covered calls, with zero open-market buying recorded. The fundamentals and the insider tape are telling two different stories.
items.tweetB: Ernie Garcia II collected $272M in premium selling covered calls at $450-500 strikes post-split. Not bearish by itself -- insiders monetize concentrated positions all the time -- but it does cap how much upside conviction you should read into a fundamentals-only bull case here.

items.title: One tactical fund claims +0.88% edge over the indices on FOMC day
items.idea: Norseman's Berserker Fund (an all-cap long/short index strategy) posted +0.88% 'EDGE' versus the major indices on today's FOMC-day selloff, per the fund's portfolio update.
items.angle: Mostly a subscription teaser, but the framing -- outperforming on the day the Fed spoke and the S&P fell -1.5% -- is a small data point worth logging for which tactical strategies are actually managing this volatility.
items.tweetA: One tactical long/short fund claims +0.88% edge over the indices on FOMC day, while the S&P fell -1.5% and the Nasdaq-100 hit correction territory. Small sample, but worth tracking which strategies are actually managing this volatility versus just riding beta down.
items.tweetB: Beating the index by less than 1% on a day the index fell 1.5% isn't alpha by itself -- it's being underweight beta into a selloff. Worth asking what specifically they were short, not just the headline number.

items.title: S&P 500's PEG ratio is the lowest in 30+ years
items.idea: The S&P 500 now has its lowest PEG ratio (price/earnings-to-growth) in over 30 years, per a linked Daily Chartbook piece -- meaning that despite elevated absolute P/E multiples, forward earnings growth expectations are high enough that the growth-adjusted valuation is actually historically cheap.
items.angle: The single most important valuation counter-data-point to the 'AI trade is stretched' theme dominating the rest of this window -- only the headline came through in the digest, worth opening the full piece.
items.tweetA: S&P 500 PEG ratio: lowest in 30+ years. Every other headline this week says stocks are priced for perfection. PEG says the market isn't pricing in nearly enough of the earnings growth that's already been guided. One of these framings is wrong.
items.tweetB: P/E says expensive. PEG says cheapest in three decades. The entire 'is the market overvalued' debate collapses into which of those two ratios you trust more -- and almost nobody arguing about valuation right now is being explicit about that choice.
